W3097637381.title: Multistage work hardening assisted by multi-type twinning in ultrafine-grained heterostructural eutectic high-entropy alloys

card: Paper card. Question: How do individual deformation mechanisms compete or synergize during plastic deformation in high-entropy alloys at ultralow temperatures, and what is the specific deformation pathway activated?. System: Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 (Cantor alloy), Cr25Fe25Co25Ni25, and Cr33.3Co33.3Ni33.3 (atomic %). Processing: Arc melting of pure elements (>99.9% purity) in Ti-gettered argon, remelted 8 times, drop-cast into Cu molds, homogenized at 1200°C for 24 hours, cold rolled to ~80% reduction, recrystallized at 800°C for 1 hour, and quenched in iced water to achieve ~5 μm grain size; tensile specimens prepared by electrical discharge machining.. Test conditions: In situ neutron diffraction under tensile loading at 15 K, 140 K, and room temperature; strain rate of 2.67 × 10−5 s−1 (0.04 mm/min) in the plastic regime; vacuum ~10−5 kPa.. Findings: At 15 K, the alloy exhibited an extraordinarily high strength of ~2.5 GPa combined with ~62% ductility.; Serrated deformation characterized by sharp load drops began beyond 21% strain, with amplitudes approaching 570 MPa near the ultimate tensile strength.; Stacking fault probability (SFP) developed early at stress > 1075 MPa and increased to 27 × 10−3 before fracture, whereas SFP was almost zero at room temperature.; The deformation pathway at 15 K followed a sequence: dislocation slip (yielding at ~718 MPa) → stacking faults (at ~1075 MPa) → twinning and serrations (at ~1270 MPa).; The (220)//LD diffraction peak disappeared almost entirely toward the end of deformation, indicating significant texture development.; The strain-hardening rate at 15 K was stable until fracture, unlike at 295 K where it decreased with deformation.; Fracture occurred via two shear bands at ~90° angles with no significant necking, despite 62% true strain.. Mechanism: The extreme work hardening and large ductility result from the cooperation of multiple deformation mechanisms: dislocation slip initiates deformation, followed by stacking faults and twinning which create additional boundaries that impede dislocation propagation. Stacking faults act as a critical bridge preventing a direct transition to serration-induced failure. The low stacking fault energy and the stability of the face-centered cubic structure at ultralow temperatures, enabled by high-entropy alloying, facilitate this pathway. Local disorder from the multicomponent nature prevents the propagation of serration flow, allowing continued strengthening until major shear bands form.. Limitations: The thermocouples were located at the sample grips rather than on the sample gauge section, meaning there could be a delay in temperature sensing and the local temperature rise in the deformed region could be much higher than measured.. Future work: The authors suggest that insights from in situ experiments point to the role of entropy in the design of structural materials with superior properties, specifically utilizing the unique combination of complex chemistry and simple crystal structure to deploy competitive mechanisms in synergy.. Quote: "The coexistence of multiple deformation pathways raises an important question regarding how individual deformation mechanisms compete or synergize during plastic deformation."

W3199783892.title: Deformation behavior of a Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Mo medium-entropy alloy at extremely low temperatures

card: Paper card. Question: How can an FCC high-entropy alloy achieve both ultrahigh strength and satisfactory ductility simultaneously across ambient to cryogenic temperatures?. System: Fe49Mn30Co10Cr10N1 (at %) high-entropy alloy (N1), specifically in partially recrystallized (PRX) and fully recrystallized (FRX) states. Processing: Vacuum-induction melting of pure metals and MnN; hot forging at 1200°C; hot rolling at 1050°C (50% reduction); homogenization at 1200°C for 2 hours; cold rolling to 60% reduction; annealing at 700°C (PRX) or 900°C (FRX) for 3 min followed by water quenching. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at 298 K and 77 K with a strain rate of 10−3 s−1. Findings: The N1-PRX material achieved an ultrahigh yield strength of 1836 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 2048 MPa, and uniform elongation of 11.6% at 77 K.; At 298 K, the N1-PRX material exhibited a yield strength of 1170 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 1224 MPa, and uniform elongation of 8.2%.; The volume fraction of LCO laths in the RX zone increased from 6% at 4% strain to 10% at 11.6% strain during cryogenic deformation.; The average diameter of LCO domains in RX grains increased from 0.31 nm (initial) to 0.51 nm after deformation at 77 K.; The LCO lath-induced strengthening contribution to yield strength at 77 K was calculated to be approximately 448 MPa (183 MPa from boundaries + 265 MPa inside laths).; The critical stress for mechanical twinning decreased from 421–438 MPa at 298 K to 318–335 MPa at 77 K.; Work-hardening rates fluctuated significantly during cryogenic deformation, with rates jumping above 4 GPa for N1-PRX and 3 GPa for N1-FRX.; The areal fraction of ε-martensite in the NRX zone increased from 0.7% at 1% strain to 6.0% after fracture (11.6% strain).. Mechanism: The authors propose that interstitial-driven local chemical order (LCO) dynamically evolves during cryogenic deformation, where LCO domains grow from short-range order (SRO) to medium-range order (MRO) within laths formed from planar-slip bands. This evolution increases lattice friction and local stacking fault energy (SFE), which hinders planar slip and promotes frequent dislocation cross-slip. The combined activation of transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP), twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP), and the dynamic refinement of microstructure by evolving LCO laths leads to exceptional work hardening and ductility alongside ultrahigh strength.. Future work: The authors suggest that the LCO-dominated microstructural design concept can be extended to more alloy classes, such as advanced steels and BCC MEAs/HEAs, where LCO can be dynamically regulated to impact mechanical performances.. Findings: The HEA manifests three distinct ferromagnetic orderings at 1084, 214, and 168 K; The emergence of the 214 K transition is attributed to the influence of the C14 phase; The high-temperature ordering at 1084 K is associated with the fcc phase, which exhibits an additional ferromagnetic ordering at 168 K; The coercive field of the fcc phase attains 667 Oe at 400 K; Electronic structure calculations substantiate the presence of ferromagnetic ground states in both phases; The Ms values at 50 K for both phases closely align with the theoretical magnetic moments. card: Paper card. Question: How can High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) be designed and optimized to simultaneously achieve high saturation magnetization, high electrical resistivity, and high malleability for soft magnetic material applications?. System: FeCoNi(AlSi)x where x ranges from 0 to 0.8 in molar ratio (alloys denoted A0 to A8). Processing: Arc-melting pure elements (>99.5 wt.% purity) in high-purity argon atmosphere on a water-cooled Cu hearth, remelted four times for homogeneity; rapid solidification into ingots; compressive testing of cylindrical samples (Φ3 × 6 mm) at room temperature with a strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1. Test conditions: Room temperature compressive testing; X-ray diffraction (30 kV, 20 mA, Cu target, 10°/min); Electrical resistivity measurement; Magnetization curves via Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS); SEM-EDS microstructural analysis. Findings: The optimal balance of properties is achieved at x = 0.2 (A2 alloy) with saturation magnetization of 1.15 T, coercivity of 1,400 A/m, electrical resistivity of 69.5 μΩ·cm, yield strength of 342 MPa, and strain without fracture of 50%.; Saturation magnetization (Ms) drops almost monotonically from 1.315 T at x = 0 (A0) to 0.46 T at x = 0.8 (A8) upon Al and Si addition.; Alloys with x ≤ 0.2 exhibit a single-phase FCC solid solution, while x = 0.3 shows a BCC + FCC mixture, and x ≥ 0.4 transitions to almost entirely BCC structure.; Plastic deformation (εp) exceeds 50% without fracture for x in the range of 0 to 0.2, whereas ductility diminishes significantly for x ≥ 0.4, with A8 shattering immediately after elastic deformation.; Electrical resistivity generally increases from x = 0 to x = 0.8, reaching 69.5 μΩ·cm at x = 0.2, which falls within the typical range (50–80 μΩ·cm) of silicon steels.; The A3 alloy (x = 0.3) exhibits a yield strength of 938 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 2,857 MPa with 33% plasticity, attributed to the mixture of FCC and BCC phases.; Coercivity (Hc) is low for x ≤ 0.2 but increases dramatically at x = 0.3 due to phase boundaries hindering domain-wall movement, before falling back at x = 0.5.. Mechanism: High saturation magnetization in FCC structures is attributed to higher atomic packing density (more ferromagnetic atoms per unit volume) and the absence of anti-parallel magnetic coupling elements like Cr; electrical resistivity increases due to lattice distortion from Al/Si, chemical randomness acting as point defects, and electron scattering; mechanical strength and malleability are governed by the phase composition (FCC favors plasticity, BCC increases lattice resistance) and solid-solution strengthening from lattice distortion.. Limitations: The text notes that for x ≥ 0.4, ductility diminishes and samples become brittle; the A8 alloy shatters immediately after elastic deformation; coercivity is highly sensitive to microstructure and difficult to predict solely from composition; ab initio calculations systematically overestimate saturation magnetization compared to experiments due to limited system size and ignored impurities/phase segregation.. Future work: The authors suggest that coercivity can be tuned within a wide range at a given composition by controlling quenching rates and applying heat/pressure treatments to further reduce Hc; the insights on composition-dependent structures and properties can guide the design of structural and functional HEAs and the development of high-entropy soft magnetic materials.. Quote: "the optimal balance of magnetic, electrical, and mechanical properties is achieved at x = 0.2, for which the combination of saturation magnetization (1.15 T), coercivity (1,400 A/m), electrical resistivity (69.5 μΩ·cm), yield strength (342 MPa), and strain without fracture (50%) makes the alloy an excellent SMM."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the structural, magnetic, and transport properties of the new equimolar high-entropy alloy FeRhIrPdPt, and how do its dual-phase microstructure and constituent binary alloys explain its magnetic behavior?. System: FeRhIrPdPt (equimolar), FeRh4, FeIr4, FePd4, FePt4. Processing: Arc melting of constituent elements (Fe, Rh, Ir, Pd, Pt) with 99.9% purity in an Ar atmosphere to form 1.5 g button-shaped samples, followed by quenching on a water-chilled Cu hearth and multiple remelting cycles for homogeneity; no heat treatment or deformation applied.. Test conditions: XRD with Cu-Kα radiation; SEM/EDX at room temperature; DC magnetic susceptibility (χdc) between 50–450 K and 2 K; AC magnetic susceptibility (χac) between 3–300 K at frequencies 20 Hz–5 kHz; Electrical resistivity (ρ) between 3–300 K using a dc four-probe method.. Findings: The alloy forms a dual-phase fcc structure with a Rh- and Ir-rich main phase (70 vol.%) and a Pd- and Pt-rich minor phase (30 vol.%).; The main phase is responsible for a canonical spin-glass transition at approximately 90 K.; The minor phase is responsible for a ferromagnetic correlation that appears below 300 K.; FeRh4 and FeIr4 binary alloys exhibit spin-freezing behavior, while FePd4 and FePt4 are ferromagnetic with Curie temperatures of ~400 K and ~317 K, respectively.; The effective magnetic moment (μeff) for FeRhIrPdPt is 3.40 μB/Fe, with a positive Weiss temperature (ΘCW) of 308 K indicating FM correlation.; The Mydosh parameter K for FeRhIrPdPt is 0.007, classifying it as a canonical spin-glass HEA.; Electrical resistivity of FeRhIrPdPt slightly increases on cooling, indicating weak carrier localization, unlike the metallic behavior of the binary alloys.; The dual-phase formation is explained by the pairwise formation enthalpies, where Fe-Pd and Fe-Pt pairings are more robust than Fe-Rh and Fe-Ir.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the dual-phase microstructure results from the thermodynamic preference for specific binary pairings (Fe-Pd, Fe-Pt, Ir-Rh) based on negative formation enthalpies. The magnetic properties arise from the independent contributions of the two phases: the Rh/Ir-rich main phase (analogous to FeRh4/FeIr4) drives the spin-glass transition at 90 K, while the Pd/Pt-rich minor phase (analogous to FePd4/FePt4) drives the ferromagnetic correlation below 300 K. The lack of long-range ordering in the ferromagnetic correlation is attributed to the inhomogeneous magnetic state of the minor phase.. Limitations: The study was limited to as-cast samples without heat treatment or deformation; the thermal stability of the dual-phase microstructure was not investigated.. Future work: The authors state it is important to understand the thermal stability of the alloy to control the microstructure, and to investigate the possibility of multifunctional magnetic properties where the two phases offer different functions.. Quote: "The dual-phase is composed of a Rh- and Ir-rich main phase and a Pd- and Pt-rich minor one."
